![Ilya Sutskever's Test of Time talk at NeurIPS 2024. [Watch on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WQQdd6qGxNs)](cover.jpg){fig-align="center"}

[Ilya Sutskever's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilya_Sutskever) [Test of Time](https://blog.neurips.cc/2024/11/27/announcing-the-neurips-2024-test-of-time-paper-awards/) award talk at [NeurIPS 2024](https://neurips.cc/Conferences/2024), accepting the prize for [*Sequence to Sequence Learning with Neural Networks*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.3215) [[1]](#ref-1) (Sutskever, [Oriol Vinyals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oriol_Vinyals), and [Quoc Le](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quoc_V._Le), 2014). The main points:

* [**Pre-training is ending**](#ch-pretraining-will-end) because compute keeps growing (better hardware, algorithms, larger clusters), but the internet doesn't. Sutskever calls data [the fossil fuel of AI](#ch-data-not-growing) and says we've hit peak.

* [**What comes next**](#ch-what-comes-next) is some mix of agents, synthetic data, and inference-time compute — phrases people are reaching for. [o1](#ch-what-comes-next) is the most vivid example so far of what's after pre-training. (Karpathy later picks up the agents thread, calling 2025–2034 ["the decade of agents"](/posts/20251018-karpathy-agi-decade-away/) on the same Dwarkesh podcast.)

* [**Reasoning is unpredictable**](#ch-long-term). Past deep learning replicated human intuition (the 0.1-second reaction time) and was therefore predictable. Reasoning systems get more unpredictable the more they reason — Sutskever cites superhuman [chess engines](#ch-long-term) as the existing precedent. (The counter-thesis is [Carina Hong's argument](/posts/20260514-carina-hong-axiom-math-is-agi/) that formal math is the missing deterministic pillar under a probabilistic LLM stack.)

* [**Biology offers a precedent for different scaling**](#ch-from-nature). Hominids sit on a different brain-to-body slope than other mammals. Evolution found at least one alternative scaling path, suggesting AI scaling needn't follow only the regime we've already figured out. ([Chollet arrives at a similar conclusion](/posts/20250707-chollet-how-we-get-to-agi/) from a different direction, arguing AGI needs both type-1 and type-2 abstractions, with type-1 scaling alone insufficient.)

For the third point it's also the nature of discrete math problems: they scale poorly due to their combinatorial nature. Solving them often requires different strategies.

The talk runs about 17 minutes plus a 7-minute Q&A. I've added an **[enriched transcript](#transcript) at the bottom of this post** built from the YouTube auto-captions, with chapter anchors, light editorial cleanup of obvious ASR mishearings, hyperlinks on first mention, and a few editor's-note callouts. See the preamble of that section for what's verbatim and what's editorial.

## Transcript

What's here is the [YouTube auto-caption track](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WQQdd6qGxNs), reorganized into a reader-friendly form. The dialog itself is verbatim — no words added, cut, or reworded — but four layers of editorial structure have been added on top:

- **Chapter outline.** The 18 official YouTube chapter markers become H3 headings, each linking to its timestamp. Inside the longer chapters I've added 17 H4 sub-headings to break out salient topic shifts. The full outline is in the right-hand sidebar. Punctuation, capitalization, and paragraph breaks are mine — the auto-captions ship without them. Obvious ASR mishearings of proper nouns and technical terms (`new RPS` → NeurIPS, `oral vineel and qule` → Oriol Vinyals and Quoc Le, `lsdm` → LSTM, `reset` → ResNet, `Alec mode` → Alec Radford, `engrams` → n-grams) are corrected silently.
- **Inline hyperlinks.** First mention of each salient acronym, paper, person, or concept links to the most authoritative source.
- **Bracketed acronym expansions.** Where an acronym appears for the first time without being expanded in speech, the expansion is inserted in `[square brackets]` to mark the addition as editorial.
- **Editor's notes** in blue callout boxes flag claims that are verifiable and slightly off, heuristics Sutskever himself qualifies as speculation, or unsourced figures.

Because YouTube's chapter markers were placed by the uploader rather than at speaker pause points, several boundaries cut mid-sentence, but these are kept faithful to the source. The lecture body (chapters 1–13) is a Sutskever monologue, so per-paragraph speaker prefixes are omitted there. The Q&A (chapters 14–18) labels each turn.

::: {.callout-note}
**Editor's note.** The Seq2Seq paper itself used a 4-layer LSTM with 1000 cells per layer (per [§3.2 of the paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.3215) [[1]](#ref-1)), not 10. Sutskever's "10 layers" is best read as the era's general training ceiling — contemporary vision networks like [VGG](https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.1556) [[2]](#ref-2) and [GoogLeNet](https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.4842) [[3]](#ref-3) reached 16–22 layers in 2014 with auxiliary tricks — rather than the specific architecture being honored.
:::

### [0:08:45 — The age of pre-training will end due to that the data is not growing](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WQQdd6qGxNs&t=525s) {#ch-data-not-growing}

::: {.callout-note}
**Editor's note.** The "peak data" / "fossil fuel of AI" framing is Sutskever's metaphor and is contested. Web text alone may be plateauing for high-quality slices, but new training corpora continue to expand: video and multimodal data, [synthetic and self-play data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.10560) [[9]](#ref-9), and RL-generated trajectories from environments. The end-of-pretraining claim is best read as a directional take from a leader of OpenAI's pretraining era, not a settled fact.
:::

The things that we are doing, the things that we've been scaling so far, is actually the first thing that we figured out how to scale. ::: {.callout-note}
**Editor's note.** The brain-to-body scaling slope shift across hominids is a real finding from comparative neuroanatomy — the relevant literature is on the [encephalization quotient](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Encephalization_quotient) and the [allometric slope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allometry) for primates vs. other mammals. Sutskever doesn't cite the source slide. The canonical reference is [Jerison (1973)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/book/9780123852502/evolution-of-the-brain-and-intelligence) [[10]](#ref-10) and follow-ons by Schoenemann and [Herculano-Houzel](https://www.suzanaherculanohouzel.com/lab-publications). The point that hominids deviate from the mammalian norm is well-established. The talk's framing of it as a "different scaling" precedent for AI is rhetorical.
:::

#### Agentic, reasoning, and unpredictable

Those systems are actually going to be agentic in real ways — whereas right now the systems are not agents in any meaningful sense, just very — that might be too strong, they're very, very slightly agentic, just beginning. It will actually reason.

And by the way, I want to mention something about reasoning, [which] is that a system that reasons — the more it reasons, the more unpredictable it becomes. The more it reasons, the more unpredictable it becomes.

All the deep learning that we've been used to is very predictable, because if you've been working on replicating human intuition, essentially, it's like the gut — if you come back to the 0.1-second reaction time, what kind of processing we do in our brains — well, it's our intuition. So we've endowed ourselves with some of that intuition.

But reasoning — you're seeing some early signs of that — reasoning is unpredictable. And one reason to see that is because the chess [AIs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_chess), the really good ones, are unpredictable to the best human chess players.

#### Self-awareness, and qualitatively different systems

So we will have to be dealing with AI systems that are incredibly unpredictable. They will understand things from limited data. They will not get confused — all the things which are really big limitations. I'm not saying how, by the way, and I'm not saying when. I'm saying that it will. In the future, would it — do you think that a model given reasoning will be able to correct itself, sort of autocorrect itself, and that will be a core feature of future models, so that there won't be as many hallucinations because the model will recognize when — I maybe that's too esoteric of a question — but the model will be able to reason and understand when a hallucination is occurring? I mean, you should check — I mean, for, yeah — it's, I wouldn't, I wouldn't rule out that it might already be happening with some of the, you know, early reasoning models of today. I don't know. My name is [Shalev Lifshitz](https://openreview.net/profile?id=~Shalev_Lifshitz1) from [University of Toronto](https://www.utoronto.ca/) working with [Sheila McIlraith](https://www.cs.toronto.edu/~sheila/). Thanks for all the work you've

### [0:22:23 — Q4: Do LLMs generalize multi-hop reasoning out of distribution?](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WQQdd6qGxNs&t=1343s) {#ch-q4}

**Audience:** [continuing] done. I wanted to ask: do you think LLMs generalize multi-hop reasoning out of distribution?

**Sutskever:** So okay, the question assumes that the answer is yes or no, but the question should not be answered with yes or no, because what does it mean — out-of-distribution generalization, what does it mean? What does it mean *in* distribution, and what does it mean *out of* distribution?

Because it's a test-of-time talk, I'll say that long, long ago — before people were using deep learning — they were using things like string matching, [n-grams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/N-gram) for [machine translation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Machine_translation). People were using statistical phrase tables.

Can you imagine, they had tens of thousands of[lines of] code of complexity, which was — I mean, it's, it was truly unfathomable. And back then, generalization meant: is it literally not in the same phrasing as in the data set?

Now we may say, well, my model achieves this high score on, um, I don't know, math competitions. But maybe the math — maybe some discussion in some forum on the internet was about the same ideas, and therefore it's memorized. Well, okay, you could say maybe it's in distribution, maybe it's memorization. But I also think that our standards for what counts as generalization have increased really quite substantially, dramatically, unimaginably, if you keep track.

::: {.callout-tip}
**Related.** Sutskever's "maybe it's memorization" hedge is the same question I [picked apart earlier](/posts/20230416-agi-llm-memorization/): claims of AGI-level LLM performance need a memorization check before they count as reasoning.
:::

And so I think, then, [the] answer is: to some degree, probably not as well as human beings. I think it is true that human beings generalize much better. But at the same time, they definitely generalize out of distribution to some degree. I hope it's a useful, topological answer.

**Audience:** Thank you. And unfortunately we're out of time for this session. I have a feeling we could go on for the next six hours, uh, but thank you so much, Ilya, for the talk. [Applause]
